content:
香港政府在大埔火灾一周年之前宣布，不会举办任何官方纪念活动，同时公布了针对悲剧受害者的新补贴计划。 2025年12月10日，一束鲜花被留在大埔宏福苑附近的路边。2025年11月26日，一场致命大火，吞没了该住宅区八个街区中的七个。照片：何凯莉/HKFP。政务司司长陈家伟周二在商业电台表示，当局不会举办任何活动哀悼火灾遇难者，因为社区已经开展了各种活动，包括宗教团体组织的活动。陈补充说，政府不会阻碍合法的纪念活动，并且在某些情况下会提供安排交通等协助。不过，陈敦促公众“谨慎”选择纪念活动，并指出网上有些人试图利用纪念活动“制造麻烦”。陈的这番言论是在 11 月 26 日大埔火灾一周年纪念日之前发表的。一些纪念活动的组织者似乎面临着当局的压力，一些教堂收到了警方的询问，活动突然被取消。与此同时，政府宣布为火灾受害者提供两项新的补助金，总额约为6.3亿港元，帮助他们“尽快开始新的生活”。民政及青年事务局局长麦惠文会见传媒。
民政及青年事务局局长麦家丽周二向传媒表示，在“新起点支援津贴”计划下，每间单位的业主将获发30万港元的补助金，而每名死者家属将获发20万港元的补助金。这些补助金将从宏福苑支援基金中拨出，该基金是一项政府主导的基金，已向企业和公众筹集了 45 亿港元。麦说，火灾发生一年后，支持基金“已基本用完”。该基金约28亿港元已指定用于支持政府买断受火灾影响的宏福苑住宅小区的所有物业。 “化悲痛为动力” 去年11月26日，大埔宏福苑住宅小区发生火灾。当该庄园正在进行大规模翻修工程时，它从一栋建筑开始，迅速蔓延到其他六个街区。这是该市几十年来最严重的火灾，夺去了 168 人的生命，其中包括 10 名家庭佣工，并导致数千人无家可归。调查这起致命火灾的独立委员会一个月前向政府提交了一份关于火灾原因和建议的报告。行政长官李家超在10月下旬的新闻发布会上带领高层官员宣布时任房屋署署长何温妮因火灾辞职，并根据委员会的建议采取了一系列改革措施。
布政司陈家祥。照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。陈表示，政府将全面落实火灾后成立的独立委员会提出的全部 120 项建议。他补充说，其中近 30 项建议已经推出，其余近 90% 的建议要么已准备好实施，要么已经在实施中，其中绝大多数将于明年完成。 “我也是香港人。这件事太严重了，令人心碎和悲伤……现在已经一年多了。”

【原文 English Original】
The Hong Kong government has announced ahead of the first anniversary of the fatal Tai Po fire that it will not host any official memorial activities, while unveiling new subsidy schemes for victims of the tragedy. A bouquet of flowers is left on a roadside near Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po, on December 10, 2025. A deadly blaze broke out on November 26, 2025, and engulfed seven of the eight blocks of the housing estate. Photo: Kelly Ho/HKFP. Chief Secretary for Administration Eric Chan said on Commercial Radio on Tuesday that authorities would not host any events to mourn the fire victims, as various activities, including those organised by religious groups, were already underway in the community. Chan added that the government would not obstruct legal memorial activities and would, in some cases, offer assistance such as arranging transportation. However, Chan urged the public to choose memorial activities “carefully,” noting that some people online were attempting to use memorial events to “make trouble.” Chan’s remarks came ahead of the first anniversary of the Tai Po fire on November 26. Organisers of some memorial activities have appeared to face pressure from authorities, with some churches receiving police enquiries and an event abruptly cancelled . Meanwhile, the government announced two new grants for the fire victims, totalling around HK$630 million, to help them “start a new life as soon as possible.” Secretary for Home and Youth Affairs Alice Mak meets the press. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Secretary for Home and Youth Affairs Alice Mak told the press on Tuesday that under the “New Beginning Support Grants” scheme, the owner of each flat would be offered HK$300,000, while another grant of HK$200,000 would be provided to the family of each deceased victim. The grants will be disbursed from the Support Fund for Wang Fuk Court, a government-led fund that has raised HK$4.5 billion from corporations and members of the public. Mak said that one year after the fire, the support fund “has been largely used up.” About HK$2.8 billion from the fund has been earmarked to support the government’s buyout of all property titles at the fire-hit Wang Fuk Court residential estate. ‘Channel sorrow into motivation’ On November 26 last year, a blaze broke out at the Wang Fuk Court residential estate in Tai Po. It started in one building and quickly spread to six other blocks while the estate was undergoing a large-scale renovation project. It was the deadliest blaze the city had seen in decades, claiming 168 lives, including 10 domestic workers, and leaving thousands homeless. An independent committee probing the deadly fire submitted a report on its causes and recommendations to the government a month ago. Chief Executive John Lee led top officials at a press conference in late October to announce that then-housing chief Winnie Ho had resigned over the blaze , alongside a series of reform measures based on the committee’s recommendations. Chief Secretary Eric Chan. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Chan said the government would fully implement all 120 recommendations put forward by the independent committee established following the fire. Nearly 30 of the recommendations have already been rolled out, while nearly 90 per cent of the remainder are either ready for implementation or already underway, with the vast majority set to be completed next year, he added. “I am also a Hongkonger. This incident was so severe, heartbreaking and sad… It has now been a year and our hearts are heavy. But from the perspective of the government, we should channel our sorrow into motivation for transformation, and make sure there will not be another such incident in the future,” Chan said in Cantonese.

title: Truths, Lies, and Prospects for the New Cross-Strait Security Complex in the Taiwan and Luzon Straits
zh_title: 台湾吕宋海峡新的两岸安全复合体的真相、谎言与前景
summary: 下载整期 PDF 简介 当前霍尔木兹海峡的危机表明了战略性地缘政治瓶颈如何影响全球供应链。吕宋岛和台湾海峡也不例外。曾经被学者和政治家想象为孤立和分裂的这些西太平洋阻塞点，一旦太平洋地区爆发重大冲突，就有可能损害世界经济动脉。在去年的另一篇《全球台湾简报》文章中，作者创造了“新的海峡两岸安全复合体”（NCSSC）一词来表示菲律宾的巩固地位。
content:
下载整期 PDF 简介 当前霍尔木兹海峡的危机表明了战略性地缘政治瓶颈如何影响全球供应链。吕宋岛和台湾海峡也不例外。曾经被学者和政治家想象为孤立和分裂的这些西太平洋阻塞点，一旦太平洋地区爆发重大冲突，就有可能损害世界经济动脉。在去年的另一篇《全球台湾简报》文章中，笔者创造了“新的海峡两岸安全复合体”（NCSSC）一词，以表示菲律宾巩固其群岛和海上防御：将西菲律宾海（WPS）和吕宋海峡作为共同关注点，并将吕宋海峡的未来安全与台湾海峡的安全联系起来。简而言之，NCSSC指的是两岸政治体之间发生和交叉的物质、制度和认知模式。笔者认为，国家社会保障委员会并不是一个空词。它代表了多个参与者遵守的有机行动框架：包括中华人民共和国（PRC）、台湾、菲律宾、美国和日本。该框架的一个值得注意的方面是认知方面如何影响互动的物质和制度模式。
简而言之，虽然一些行为者最近正在恢复过去的真相，即菲律宾伊瓦坦人民和台湾道族人民之间的过去联系，以塑造未来的关系，但还有一些行为者也在利用过去散布谎言。这包括中华人民共和国淡化这种联系，以及对巴丹群岛的主权声索。最终，国家安全安全委员会敦促各国和其他行为者为更广泛的印太地区的未来安全议程制定更明确的政策和灵活的机制。交互框架？众所周知，菲律宾在推行其外交和安全政策方面总是得过且过。文献争论它是否有一个深思熟虑的大战略，但有一件事是肯定的：台湾的未来现在在马尼拉的视野中，因为它看到中华人民共和国不受限制的地区野心。正如菲律宾领导人的言论和官方文件所指出的那样，“被拖入潜在的冲突”是一回事。然而，认识到其在更广泛的印度太平洋地区的地缘政治重要性是另一回事。 NCSSC 是一个合理的框架，可以了解区域参与者在近期和遥远的未来如何互动。最近发生的事件显示了这种互动的规律性。从积极的角度来看，我们可以看到台湾人和菲律宾人在历史和文化上如何通过海洋联系在一起。 2026年6月，来自台湾最南端岛屿兰屿的20名涛人驶入菲律宾最北端岛屿巴丹群岛玛哈涛的一个港口。
这是一段约 111 英里的旅程，乘坐的是名为 Tatala（陶族人所称）或 Tataya（巴丹群岛伊瓦坦人所称）的传统木船。陶人与伊瓦坦人之间如此深厚的联系——尽管由于殖民主义而休眠了 300 年——展示了该地区的当代人民如何通过复制这种 4000 年的移民和航海实践来讲述这些闻所未闻的故事。事实上，这种重燃提醒人们注意它们与南岛语系的联系。尽管缺乏高级政府官员对陶伊-伊瓦坦交流的明确支持声明，菲律宾运输安全办公室战略性地

【原文 English Original】
DOWNLOAD FULL ISSUE PDF Introduction The current crisis in the Strait of Hormuz demonstrates how strategic geopolitical chokepoints can affect the global supply chain. The Luzon and Taiwan Straits are no different. Once imagined by academics and politicians to be isolated and separated, these Western Pacific chokepoints have the potential to harm the world’s economic arteries should a major conflict erupt in the Pacific Region. In a separate Global Taiwan Brief article from last year, this author coined the term, “New Cross-Strait Security Complex” (NCSSC) to denote the Philippines’ consolidation of its archipelagic and maritime defense: interlocking the West Philippine Sea (WPS) and Luzon Strait as a common concern, and linking the Luzon Strait’s future security with that of the Taiwan Strait. Put simply, NCSSC refers to the material, institutional, and cognitive patterns occurring and intersecting between the polities of the two straits. This author argues that the NCSSC is not an empty term. It represents an organic framework of action observed by multiple actors: including the People’s Republic of China (PRC), Taiwan, the Philippines, the United States, and Japan. One notable dimension of this framework comes with how the cognitive aspect affects the material and institutional patterns of interactions. Simply put, while some actors are recently recovering truths of the past—namely, the past connection between the Philippines’ Ivatan people, and Taiwan’s Tao people—to shape the future relations, still others are also using the past to spread lies. This includes the PRC’s downplay of that connection, and claims over the Batanes Islands. Ultimately, the NCSSC impels states and other actors to produce clearer policies with flexible mechanisms for the future security agenda in the broader Indo-Pacific region. A Framework of Interaction? The Philippines is known to muddle through in pursuing its foreign and security policies. The literature debates whether or not it has a deliberate grand strategy , yet one thing is certain: the future of Taiwan is now in Manila’s sights as it sees the PRC’s regional ambitions unrestrained. “To be dragged into a potential conflict”—as noted by Philippine leaders’ rhetoric and official documents —is one thing. However, to appreciate its geopolitical importance in the broader Indo-Pacific is another. The NCSSC serves as a sensible framework to see how regional actors might interact in the immediate and distant future. Recent events show the regularity of such interaction. On a positive note, we can see how Taiwanese and Filipinos are historically and culturally linked by the seas. In June 2026, 20 Tao people from Orchid Island (Lanyu, 蘭嶼 ), Taiwan’s southernmost island, sailed into a port in Mahatao, Batanes, the Philippines’ northernmost island. This was a journey of about 111 miles using a traditional wooden boat known as Tatala (as known by the Tao people) or Tataya (as known by the Ivatans of Batanes). Such deep connections between the Taos and Ivatans—although dormant for 300 years due to colonialism—demonstrates how contemporary peoples of this region are making these unheard stories heard by replicating this 4000-year practice of migration and seafaring. Indeed, such rekindling serves as a reminder of their Austronesian linkage. Though lacking an explicit supportive statement of the Tao-Ivatan exchange by higher government officials, the Philippines’ Office for Transportation Security strategically framed its press release about Manila’s resolve to “ensure that the country’s northern maritime gateways remain protected and efficient” in the case of “welcoming communities.” Image: The Batanes Strait, between Taiwan and the northern Philippines. In 2026, PRC government institutions began to advance the claim that the Batanes Islands (part of the Philippines) were Chinese territory, based on the extension of the continental shelf from Taiwan. (Image source: Google Maps ) Interestingly, two Chinese officials— Ambassador to the Philippines Jing Quan, and Consul and Head of Post Li Xiaoyan of the Chinese Consulate in Laoag, Ilocos Norte— arrived in Batanes on the same day as the Tao people’s arrival for an “official visit” to the province’s officials. On the one hand, this visit serves to remind Philippine officials of Manila’s “One-China Policy.” On the other hand, it also means that Beijing is now playing into the logic of the NCSSC, which serves as a prognosis for broader regional tensions. Some academics from the PRC contest the “ Out of Taiwan” theory of Austronesian linkage between the Tao and Ivatan peoples. Rather, they prefer to propagate Beijing’s narrative of historic rights over Taiwan, contending that these indigenous peoples came instead from mainland southern China. In July 2026, a Global Times article reported that several PRC-based academics at an academic symposium in Jinan University ( 暨南大學 ) asserted that the Batanes Islands “are legally China’s sovereign territory and form a natural geographic extension of China’s Taiwan island,” on the basis of the 1898 Treaty of Paris and the so-called “Japan-Philippines maritime delimitation talks.” In other words, by virtue of PRC’s historic claims on Taiwan and the Tao’s linkage to the Ivatans, Batanes is allegedly an integral part of the PRC. Philippine government officials have rebuked such PRC academic’s claims on Batanes. For instance, Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. noted at the sidelines of the West Philippine Sea summit that such talking points by PRC academics validated his agency’s assessment that Beijing wants to control the Western Pacific. Moreover, given that there is no serious legal basis for such claims, Teodoro noted that “it’s a joke.” Separately, Philippine Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro noted that the government would not listen to unofficial channels, while her agency’s spokesperson Analyn Ratonel said that “flights of fancy should not be dignified with a response” since “the Philippines’ sovereignty over Batanes is settled and not up for debate.” Batanes’ lone District House Representative, Ciriaco Gato Jr., similarly rebuked such claims, noting that “any challenge to our status is not merely a geopolitical provocation; it is an affront to our identity that we will not tolerate.” The Philippine’s National Historical Commission (NHC) debunked the Chinese scholarly claims, noting that there is a continuous shelf extending from Northern Luzon through the Babuyan and Batanes Islands and into parts of the Taiwan archipelago based on “current satellite and oceanographic data.” There were also reported circulations among Chinese social media apps last year suggesting that the Philippine province of Palawan—which puts the Municipality of Kalayaan in the WPS under its jurisdiction—is allegedly part of China, by virtue of Ming-era Admiral Zheng He’s explorations. At the macro-level, the Philippine government recognizes that such Chinese talking points are reinforced by foreign influence and malign interference (FIMI) operations —various kinetic activities that aim to alter Filipino solidarity in favor of PRC’s narratives. All Set for the Future? These latest events demonstrate that the framework of interaction demonstrated by the NCSSC does not only involve material and institutional aspects, but also the most basic of human cognitive elements—identity, historical memory, and people-to-people linkage—which are all essential to make the case for brokering the regional commons. They also point to a common denominator: the PRC’s irredentist and unrestrained expansion. However, the NCSSC also opens novel methods for various stakeholders to explore opportunities to assert their agency. The first opportunity refers to cognitive patterns. Whether by constraints or deliberate choice, the Taiwanese government has yet to make any comments on the claim by PRC-based academics regarding Batanes. While ignoring Chinese talking points against the Philippines may sound risk-averse, there is an equal harm inherent in isolating these comments outside the PRC’s broader FIMI operations. Taiwan’s political and security apparatuses would be well advised to invest their attention in curating counter-responses. Moreover, both Manila and Taipei must also leverage linkages between Filipino and Taiwanese cultural communities, academics, think tanks, and civil society organizations, to counter the PRC’s FIMI operational logic. The second opportunity refers to institutional patterns. Since Taiwan is de facto limited in its diplomatic options, the Philippines—with its rapidly expanding strategic partnerships—could serve as a node of a broader security network by framing the Luzon and Taiwan Straits as strategic nerves that cannot be unilaterally occupied by one regional hegemon. Rather, the Straits represent a politically plural area in which to enforce a rules-based international order. This would mean enhancing logistical points of entry and exchange through increased port security, diversifying areas of cooperation between their respective coast guards, fisheries agreements, and anti-piracy and anti-smuggling frameworks, among others. Moreover, while Filipino and American officials argue that Balikatan exercises are solely for Philippine defense, and not intended as a stage for a Taiwan contingency, Filipino and other regional scholars and analysts otherwise note that they are not mutually exclusive. Here, wargaming centers by academics and think tanks can intensify stress-testing assumptions into wider grand strategic considerations, which ripple into Track 1.5/2 dialogues and influence public opinion. The third opportunity refers to material patterns. So far, it is microchip discourse which catches the main attention of the PRC, the US, and other global players on this NCSSC. Minilateral forums serve as cost-efficient avenues in addressing shortcomings of multilateral forums that have been hijacked by PRC’s “Global South Champion” narrative. Moreover, informal talks—like the “Smart Harbor” forum in December 2025 between Taipei and Philippine officials—demonstrate the balance between strategic autonomy and risk-aversion. The Luzon Economic Corridor, which feeds into the US’s Pax Silica initiative to counter the PRC’s World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), are both welcome developments. Taiwan has stated on separate occasions that it is willing to expand economic corridors with the Philippines, either through its proposed “ Silicon Prosperity Initiative ” or as an external node with Pax Silica . So far, Pax Silica has not been well received by most Filipinos, largely due to the lack of an accurate and transparent blueprint, which in turn caused fear among local communities. So far, the Philippines rejection of a diplomatic immunity bargain by the United States in the proposed Pax Silica compound in North Luzon are very well noted points to rebuke PRC narratives of the Philippines “as an American Puppet.” However, the broader goal must be the ability of the Philippines to become a formidable node of the global supply chain through state-led development—not “independent” for its own sake—while addressing local woes. In sum, there is a need for more assertive Philippine counterproposals to serve the country’s industrial interests if it is to become Taiwan’s capable partner. Strategic uncertainty will continue to pervade the 21 st century, and the new geopolitical reality of the NCSSC has now emerged around which all stakeholders must carefully design their approach. They must set clear policy interests while maintaining flexible mechanisms. As for the Philippines and Taiwan, they have an opportunity to set their shared path by modeling such interactions. The main point: The Philippines is becoming more relevant to the future of Taiwan’s security, as the two island states find their security concerns ever-more connected. It is time for all stakeholders to integrate the New Cross-Strait Security Complex as part of the broader regional security architecture. They should and can achieve this through clearer policies, with flexible and responsive mechanisms for future interaction. The post Truths, Lies, and Prospects for the New Cross-Strait Security Complex in the Taiwan and Luzon Straits appeared first on Global Taiwan Institute .

zh_title: 双龙：台湾和韩国如何通过芯片进行合作
summary: 下载整期 PDF 台湾和韩国是亚洲四小龙中人口和经济总量最大的两个国家，两国是激烈的竞争对手，尤其是在半导体制造业。但它们对中国市场的共同依赖已成为双方都无法单独解决的弱点。每个人都控制着全球半导体制造的关键节点，它们共同可能构成全球硬件生态系统的瓶颈。台北和首尔应该合作开拓新市场并与大国进行谈判。他们在一起拥有任何人都无法运用的影响力
content:
下载整期 PDF 台湾和韩国是亚洲四小龙中人口和经济总量最大的两个国家，两国是激烈的竞争对手，尤其是在半导体制造业。但它们对中国市场的共同依赖已成为双方都无法单独解决的弱点。每个人都控制着全球半导体制造的关键节点，它们共同可能构成全球硬件生态系统的瓶颈。台北和首尔应该合作开拓新市场并与大国进行谈判。他们在一起所拥有的影响力是任何一个人都无法单独有效地运用的。台湾和韩国是竞争对手，也是伙伴，长期以来一直是死对头。 1992年首尔从台北转而承认北京这一相对较新的记忆，给许多台湾人留下了挥之不去的背叛感，因为韩国是亚洲最后一个与台湾断绝外交关系的国家。据称，在2000年代和2010年代，韩国三星电子推行“杀台”计划，旨在削弱台湾的芯片制造能力。此外，2010年亚运会跆拳道比赛的有争议的裁判，也被称为“索克门”，严重侵蚀了双边的公众善意。 2012年，富士康创始人郭台铭在讨论与三星的竞争时，使用具有种族主义贬义的“高丽棒子”来指代韩国人，引发强烈批评，进一步助长韩国的反台情绪。
鉴于这段痛苦的历史和所涉及的非常现实的财务利益，韩国和台湾芯片公司的竞争常常被相互对抗的感觉所掩盖。过去，外部试图协调台北和首尔的芯片政策——例如总统乔·拜登的“芯片4联盟”概念——失败了，因为他们没有充分考虑台湾和韩国领先芯片制造商之间激烈竞争的逻辑。然而，不健康的竞争和民族主义不应该让任何一方蒙蔽双眼。如今，两个邻近的东亚民主国家及其制造业冠军之间的协同关系比许多人想象的要强得多。台裔英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋近期分别于5月底和6月初连续访问台湾和韩国，受到两地热烈欢迎。这样的反应说明了两国经济在当今半导体行业中的相互联系和互补程度有多深。黄先生还因其对促进美韩关系的贡献而被授予今年的詹姆斯·范弗利特奖。在经济上，亚洲邻国建立了持久的关系。 2025年，韩国是台湾第三大贸易伙伴，台湾是韩国第四大贸易伙伴。此外，两个经济体之间已经存在部分劳动分工。
台湾公司，尤其是台湾积体电路制造股份有限公司（台积电、台湾积体电路制造股份有限公司）制造先进的逻辑芯片，而韩国的三星和 SK 海力士则在存储器领域占据主导地位。这些公司（以及两国）是当今人工智能革命不可或缺的一部分，无论是在训练人工智能模型还是为数据中心提供服务方面。到2025年，两国经济体的双边芯片贸易额将超过600亿美元，其中台湾的先进逻辑芯片支持韩国人工智能计算基础设施的快速发展，而台湾则封装了许多韩国制造的高带宽内存（HBM）芯片。 2025年台湾进口额约493亿美元

DOWNLOAD FULL ISSUE PDF Taiwan and South Korea, the two largest of the Four Asian Dragons by population and economic output, are fierce rivals, especially in the semiconductor manufacturing industry. But their common reliance on China’s market has become a vulnerability that neither can address alone. Each controls crucial nodes of global semiconductor manufacturing, and together they could constitute a chokepoint in the global hardware ecosystem. Taipei and Seoul should collaborate to open new markets and negotiate with major powers. Together, they have leverage that neither one can wield so effectively alone. Rivals, but Also Partners Taiwan and South Korea have long been bitter rivals. The relatively recent memory of Seoul switching recognition from Taipei to Beijing in 1992 has left a lingering sense of betrayal among many Taiwanese, as South Korea was the last country in Asia to end diplomatic relations with Taiwan. In the 2000s and 2010s, South Korea’s Samsung Electronics allegedly pursued a “kill Taiwan” plan aimed at undermining Taiwan’s chipmaking capabilities. Furthermore, the contested judgment in the taekwondo competition at the 2010 Asian Games, also called “ Sockgate ,” sharply eroded bilateral public goodwill. In 2012, Foxconn founder Terry Gou (郭台銘), while discussing competition with Samsung, used the derogatory racist slur, gaoli bangzi (高麗棒子), to refer to Koreans, prompting strong criticism and further fueling anti-Taiwanese sentiment in South Korea. Given this bitter history and the very real financial stakes involved, the South Korean and Taiwanese chip firm rivalry is often shaded by feelings of mutual antagonism. In the past, outside attempts to align Taipei and Seoul’s chip policies—such as President Joe Biden’s “Chip 4 Alliance” concept —fell short because they did not adequately reckon with the logic of heated competition between leading Taiwanese and South Korean chipmakers. However, unhealthy rivalry and nationalism should not blind either side. The two neighboring East Asian democracies, together with their manufacturing champions, have a far more synergistic relationship today than many assume. Taiwanese American Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s (黃仁勳) recent consecutive visits to Taiwan and South Korea in late May and early June, respectively, garnered warm welcomes in both places. Such a reaction speaks to how deeply interconnected and complementary the two economies have become in today’s semiconductor industry. Huang was also awarded this year’s James A. Van Fleet Award for his contributions to the promotion of US-South Korea relations. Economically, the Asian neighbors have built enduring ties. In 2025, South Korea was Taiwan’s third-largest trading partner, while Taiwan was South Korea’s fourth-largest . Furthermore, a partial division of labor already exists between the two economies. Taiwanese firms, notably Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC, 台灣積體電路製造股份有限公司), manufacture advanced logic chips , while South Korea’s Samsung and SK Hynix dominate memory. These companies (and both countries) are integral to today’s AI revolution, both for training AI models and supplying data centers. The two economies conducted over USD 60 billion in bilateral chip trade in 2025, with Taiwan’s advanced logic chips supporting rapid AI compute infrastructure development in South Korea, while Taiwan packages many South Korean-made high bandwidth memory (HBM) chips. In 2025, Taiwan imported around USD 49.3 billion worth of integrated circuits from South Korea, representing 37.7 percent of Taiwan’s chip imports, far more than from any other country. South Korea accounted for a smaller but still significant share of Taiwan’s integrated circuit exports , around USD 18.4 billion, or 8.8 percent. Shared Challenges Yet despite this growing industrial interdependence, Taiwan and South Korea remain exposed to the same strategic vulnerability: both of them depend heavily on China as a major downstream market for their chips. China’s booming electronics industry consumes vast quantities of semiconductor chips for everything from iPhones to appliances to AI data centers. In 2025, 51.2 percent of Taiwan’s chip exports went to mainland China or Hong Kong, while 41.7 percent of South Korean chip exports headed to the PRC. Such overwhelming reliance on one market—especially one that is actively subsidizing its own domestic chip manufacturers to gradually reduce foreign dependence—carries substantial economic security risk. SK Hynix, Samsung, and TSMC may eventually lose much of China’s demand to state-backed Chinese firms. Moreover, Beijing’s increasingly aggressive security posture and willingness to coerce smaller economies make China a fundamentally unreliable customer. Taiwan and South Korea have long recognized this problem, and each has pursued its own trade reorientation over the past decade. Taipei launched the “New Southbound Policy” under former president Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文) in 2016. Seoul followed in 2017 by initiating its “New Southern Policy” under then-president Moon Jae-in. These policies succeeded in deepening economic relations with other markets—especially those in Southeast Asia—but have failed to fundamentally reorient chip exports away from China. At the time, the political impetus and market opportunities were simply insufficient. Image: A semiconductor chip manufactured by SK Hynix, one of South Korea’s major chip manufacturers. Taiwan and South Korea manufacturers have faced intense competition qin the market for advanced chips. (Image source: Wikimedia Commons ) How to Team Up Through Chips Today, Seoul and Taipei cannot afford to go it alone. Reducing the relative weight of the Chinese market for their chip exports is not only a security imperative; it is an economic necessity as China’s indigenous chip ecosystem gains ground . Building on the complementary strengths of their semiconductor industries, South Korea and Taiwan could establish an industry-led bilateral working group led by their chip giants—TSMC, Samsung, and SK Hynix—to coordinate semiconductor trade and investment policy. Given the absence of formal diplomatic relations, a direct government-to-government framework with ministerial leadership would not be realistic. However, the sheer economic and monetary weight of these private firms and their close ties to their respective governments would give a cooperative framework substantial influence and credibility. For instance, Taiwan’s National Development Fund is a major shareholder in TSMC, while TSMC founder and former CEO Morris Chang led Taiwan’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) delegation seven times between 2006 and 2023. Similarly, given its strong relationships with Korean chip firms, the Lee Jae Myung administration has a record of leveraging its commercial involvement to pursue decisive political objectives . For instance, ahead of the August 2026 election in South Korea for Democratic Party leadership, Lee promoted a major semiconductor cluster in Jeolla Province backed by planned investment from Samsung and SK Hynix. The initiative benefited one of Lee’s cabinet officials, Kim Min-seok, helping him win the election for party leader to replace Lee’s prominent rival within the party, Jung Chung-rae. Critics accused the administration of using corporate investment to tilt politics in Lee’s favor. Yet, this example demonstrates that Seoul maintains substantial influence over its domestic semiconductor industry—and could work effectively with those firms to facilitate de facto economic collaboration with their Taiwanese counterparts that prioritizes national rather than private interests. Similarly, TSMC — which was established with Taipei’s financial and political backing in 1987 — retains close ties to Taiwan’s political leadership. Taiwanese and South Korean industry associations and companies would provide the institutional backbone of the working group and serve as the primary channel for bilateral engagement, with which the governments could easily and regularly engage. Trade and economic government officials could participate discreetly at the working level or through the two sides’ representative offices. More senior officials would have the opportunity to speak directly in private meetings alongside multilateral institutions in which both are represented, such as the APEC, to coordinate the working group. Some level of unofficial government contact is prudent to ensure that the nominally private sector working group advances the interests of South Korea and Taiwan as a whole, as well as those of their chip firms. This working group would have two primary aims: (1) to develop a common strategy to cultivate new markets; and (2) to coordinate negotiations on new trade and investment agreements with major economies from a position of greater strength. One Strategy, One Face Taiwanese and South Korean chips flow primarily to three sectors: cloud computing infrastructure; consumer goods such as electronics , appliances and automobiles ; and telecommunications equipment. Yet China’s massive output in all three categories has created a gravitational pull that has been hard for Taiwanese and Korean chip firms to escape. As a result, any joint Taiwan-South Korea strategy for cultivating overseas markets and negotiating trade agreements must go beyond setting up chip packaging facilities or even fabs. They must push for a broader set of economic reforms in those markets that will facilitate the rapid development of consumer electronics manufacturing and cloud computing infrastructure. India holds the most potential. Unlike in Southeast Asia , Chinese investment and 5G telecommunications penetration are fairly low , and the country has massive room for growth. Individual Taiwanese and South Korean firms such as Foxconn, Samsung, and Hyundai have had success with particular projects that received special Indian government attention and support. Indeed, the Indian government has repeatedly identified electronics, automobiles, and semiconductors as key sectors to bolster India’s manufacturing output. But India’s complex regulatory environment, bureaucratic proceduralism, infrastructure development bottlenecks, and sometimes counterproductive labor laws mean that India’s operating environment remains very difficult for foreign investors. [1] As a result, India has failed to generate an electronics manufacturing ecosystem—and chip demand—that can rival China’s. By speaking with one voice to New Delhi as the only two economies capable of helping fulfill India’s ambitions in electronics and semiconductor manufacturing, Seoul and Taipei might make greater progress in pressing for reforms in India than either could alone. They might also open greater access for Taiwanese and South Korean firms to a more populated market than China—one which has yet to expend its demographic dividend. The same logic applies to Taiwan’s and South Korea’s policies vis-à-vis the United States. In recent years, successive US administrations have pressed Taiwanese and South Korean chipmakers to expand manufacturing on American soil, from the Biden Administration’s CHIPS and Science Act to the Trump Administration’s greater demands for investments in the United States. Washington’s desire to reshore enough chip production to sustain its defense capabilities and economic system in a supply shock is a rational pursuit. However, as long as key inputs, downstream packaging, and testing still occur outside of the United States, domestic chip fabrication alone is inadequate to ensure US economic resilience. Moreover, a substantial share of the world’s chips still end up in electronics made in Asia. Even if the United States can ensure a bare minimum supply at home for military use and cloud services providers, it will have to look beyond its borders for sufficient demand to make US chip production economical in the long run. Image: Then-President Joseph Biden and then-President Yoon Suk-yeol visiting a Samsung semiconductor plant in South Korea (May 2022), (Image source: Wikimedia Commons ) More recent US administrations have focused on boosting foreign investment in the United States. A Washington willing to subordinate political and geostrategic partnerships in favor of a maximum reshoring effort might seek to play Taipei and Seoul against each other by inducing them to pledge ever greater semiconductor investments. This tactic could gradually hollow out the manufacturing capacity underpinning their respective “silicon shields,” leaving both more vulnerable to security threats from China in the long run — even if the most advanced logic chips are still produced in Taiwan. Instead of competing to offer ever-larger investments and concessions, Taipei and Seoul should coordinate the scale, terms, and technological scope of their US investments. Rather than sending an ultimatum to Washington, Taipei and Seoul could provide a roadmap for a sustained Taiwan-South Korea-US trilateral partnership on semiconductor innovation and fabrication to support US-led AI stack dominance (which covers the whole production chain from critical minerals and energy to semiconductors and telecommunications equipment, upon which the development and rollout of AI software relies). This triangle would be based on mutual trust and common economic and security interests. This would be far more beneficial to all involved—including the United States—than haphazard investment pledges. Targeted investments would complement ongoing economic security projects (such as the Hanwha Philly Shipyard in Philadelphia ) and help anchor chip fab suppliers in the United States. They would also allow Taiwanese and South Korean chip firms to better serve their US customers; indeed, this was part of the rationale that made the initial TSMC plant in Arizona feasible. More direct cooperation between Taipei, Seoul, and Washington may also allow all three parties to identify and capitalize on new production synergies of which US policymakers may not be aware. The main point : Ongoing commercial rivalry and nationalist sentiments show that the Taiwan-South Korea partnership will not be easy. But in continuing to work alone—and sometimes at odds—Taipei and Seoul are leaving leverage on the table that could secure their symbiotic prosperity for years to come. [1] Devesh Kapur and Arvind Subramanian, A Sixth of Humanity: Independent India’s Development Odyssey (Gurugram: HarperCollins Publishers India, 2025). 下载整期 PDF 封面图片：台北市长电视辩论主办方提供照片（来源：记者） 编者注：这是两部分系列中的第二篇文章。第一篇文章《首都之战：2026年台北市长竞选内幕（上）》于10月30日发表。作为现任台北市长的中国国民党蒋万安面临着与民进党提名候选人沈伯洋连任的巨大压力。尽管他们的背景和公众形象相似，但他们的政治声誉、政策问题立场和竞选风格却截然不同。随着11月28日大选（台湾规模较大的“九合一”地方选举的一部分）临近，全岛都在关注“洋流”或“洋流”（见下文）是否会导致未来四年不同的政治格局。竞争候选人的背景 作为目前国内外关注焦点的台北市长竞选的两位领先候选人，蒋和沉在经历和公众形象方面有一些惊人的相似之处。蒋和沈都与台北有着深厚的渊源，因为他们都在这座城市长大，并就读于著名的建国中学，该中学被誉为台湾最好的男子高中。
他们杰出的高等教育背景也强化了他们的精英形象：蒋获得了宾夕法尼亚大学法学硕士学位（LL.M.）和法学博士学位（J.D.），而沉获得了宾夕法尼亚大学法学硕士学位和法学博士学位。加州大学欧文分校犯罪学、法律和社会学位。在台湾政治中，学历和教育资历起着“极其重要”的作用。台湾的竞选广告牌、传单和其他宣传材料往往侧重于突出候选人的教育资历而不是其他特征，因为许多台湾选民将候选人的教育水平和母校的声望视为其执政能力的指标。台湾知名政界人士大多至少拥有硕士学位，而拥有博士学位的人竞选立法或市长级别的公职也很常见。因此，毫不奇怪，在2026年竞选台北市长的六名候选人中，其中五人拥有博士学位。学位或法学博士（第六名候选人拥有硕士学位）。此外，蒋、沈均是各自政党的中年一代，年龄相近，政治履历也较新。
国民党和民进党的重要人物均年龄偏大，据观察，当地政客的平均年龄正在增加。相比之下，两位台北市长候选人被认为是各自政党的“新鲜血液”。 2015年当选立委，2020年赢得台北市长选举；沉在2023年首次进入立法院。无论2026年的选举结果如何，他们都将成为未来十年各自政治阵营中的后起之秀。尽管有上述共同点，两人的政治声誉和道路却截然不同。例如，蒋介石的家族关系

DOWNLOAD FULL ISSUE PDF Cover i mage: Photo provided by the Taipei Mayoral Television Debate organizers (Source: The Reporter ) Editor’s Note: This is the second article in a two-part series. The first article, “ Battle for the Capital: Inside the 2026 Taipei Mayoral Race, Part 1 ,” was published by GTI on October 30. As the incumbent Taipei mayor, Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) of the Kuomintang (KMT, 中國國民黨) faces immense pressure to succeed in his re-election bid against Puma Shen ( 沈伯洋 ), the candidate nominated by the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP, 民主進步黨). Despite the similarities in their backgrounds and public image, their political reputations, stances on policy issues, and campaign styles set them apart. As the election (part of Taiwan’s larger “Nine-in-One” local elections) approaches on November 28, the whole island is watching whether the “Ocean Current,” or “Yang Liu” (洋流) (see further below) , will lead to a different political landscape over the next four years. The Background of the Competing Candidates As the two leading candidates in the Taipei mayoral race—a race now at the center of national and international attention—Chiang and Shen share a few striking similarities in terms of their experience and public image. Both Chiang and Shen have deep ties to Taipei, as they both grew up in the city and attended the famous Chien Kuo High School (建國中學) that is revered as the premier high school for boys in Taiwan. Their prominent higher educational backgrounds also reinforce their elite images: Chiang obtained a Master of Laws (LL.M.) degree and a Juris Doctor (J.D.) from the University of Pennsylvania, while Shen earned a LL.M. degree from the University of Pennsylvania and a Ph.D. degree in Criminology, Law, and Society from the University of California, Irvine. In Taiwan politics, academic qualifications and educational credentials play a role of “ outsized significance . ” It is often the case that Taiwanese campaign billboards, flyers, and other promotional materials focus on highlighting the candidates’ educational credentials over other characteristics, since many Taiwanese voters view candidates’ level of education and the prestige of their alma maters as an indicator of their ability to govern. The majority of well-known Taiwan politicians hold a master’s degree a t a minimum , and it is quite common to see those with doctorate degrees running for public office at the legislative or mayoral level . Therefore, it is no surprise that, out of the six candidates running for Taipei mayor in 2026, five of them hold either a Ph.D. degree or J.D. (the sixth candidate has a master’s degree). In addition, both Chiang and Shen represent the middle-age generation of their respective political parties, sharing similar ages and relatively new political resumes. The more prominent figures of both the KMT and DPP tend to be older, and it has been observed that the average age of local politicians is increasing. In contrast, the two Taipei mayoral candidates are considered the “new blood” of their respective parties. Chiang was elected as a legislator in 2015 and won the Taipei mayor election in 2020; Shen first entered the Legislative Yuan (LY) in 2023. Regardless of the 2026 election results, both of them are set to be rising stars within their respective political camps for the next decade. In spite of the commonalities mentioned above, the two men have quite different political reputations and paths. For example, Chiang’s familial connection has been in the center of public debate for years before the current election cycle. His father, Chiang Hsiao-yen (蔣孝嚴)—who claimed to be the descendant of Chiang Kai-shek (蔣中正) and Chiang Ching-kuo (蔣經國)—was a former minister of foreign affairs and former KMT secretary general. On one hand, the Chiang family name makes the KMT candidate an insider in Taiwanese politics, and the prestige of being the fourth generation of the Chiang family has allowed Chiang Wan-an to enjoy a public reputation following his return from the United States to Taiwan. On the other hand, Chiang’s bloodline credibility has been challenged, as some doubt Chiang’s actual familial connection with Chiang Ching-kuo. Additionally, the incumbent has only apologized to victims of the White Terror (白色恐怖) in his role as Taipei mayor, while some have argued that he should bear the burden as a descendant of the former authoritarian president. Compared to Chiang’s insider status as part of a prominent political dynasty, Shen has been seen as more of a political outsider, with a previous academic career and extensive experience in the nonprofit sector. He is an associate professor in criminology at National Taipei University, with research interests in the field of white-collar crimes. In 2019, he founded the Doublethink Lab (台灣民主實驗室), an NGO analyzing informational and cognitive warfare; and Kuma Academy (黑熊學院) in 2023, a civic group advocating for civil defense. Some are concerned about Shen’s late entry to Taiwan’s politics and his relative lack of administrative experience. Others are worried that Shen’s expertise in foreign interference and brash political style could make him overly provocative for local governance. Image: Taipei mayoral candidates Chiang Wan-an of the KMT (left) and Puma Shen of the DPP (right) shake hands before their televised debate on October 31. (Image source: Central News Agency ) Salient Policy Discussions Throughout the Taipei mayoral campaign, both sides have had heated debates on various policy issues, including drug treatment , school lunch quality , tree trimming , and traffic safety . In terms of the race between Chiang and Shen, the debates surrounding child welfare and the potential relocation of Songshan Airport (松山機場) have drawn the most public attention. Songshan Airport Relocation One of Chiang’s main policy proposals is a plan to relocate Songshan Airport and replace it with a Taipei AI park. In the relocation plan , Chiang pledged to build an AI industry zone, public green space, and a sustainable community with residential areas, historical preservation sites , and transportation networks. Chiang envisioned that the new AI park would create a comprehensive industrial network by connecting with multiple neighboring technological parks: Beitou-Shilin Technology Park (北投士林科技園區), Neihu Technology Park (內湖科技園區), National Biotechnology Research Park (國家生技 研 究園區) and Nangang Software Park (南港軟體園區). The proposal estimates that, over time, the AI park would create an estimated 65 thousand job opportunities, and generate NTD 12 trillion in output value. However, there is pushback against the plan from both the central government and local governments. The Ministry of Transportation and Communication (MOTC, 交通部) has expressed concern about the feasibility of the plan, as well as air transportation capacity. If the relocation project is carried out, Taoyuan International Airport will have to take on significant additional air traffic; yet, as its original design was intended for international rather than domestic flights, it will take around 10 years to increase Taoyuan Airport’s capacity to a level necessary for the loss of Songshan. The Ministry of Interior (MOI, 內政部) has also pointed out that Songshan Airport is critical for search-and-rescue in northern Taiwan, since it also serves as the Songshan Base for the National Air Service Corps (空中勤務總隊). In addition, Penghu County and Taitung County have opposed the policy proposal, on grounds that Songshan Airport has played an important role in medical transportation for the outlying islands and eastern Taiwan. While Shen also agreed that the Songshan relocation plan is worth discussing, he emphasized the necessity to prioritize issues of national defense, medical transportation from rural areas, and disaster relief. Child Welfare Major child abuse cases during Chiang’s current mayorship have sparked public attention on both candidates’ child welfare policy. Since 2022, Taipei has seen eight serious child abuse cases and 115 minor victims. The severity of minor abuse incidents has put the Taipei City government under the spotlight. The Audit Office (審計部) of the Control Yuan (監察院) revealed that Taipei City has not incorporated the assessment system introduced by the central government into its own case screening mechanism, and up to 303 minor welfare reports have been delayed since last August. The Control Yuan has also censured the Taipei City government for negligence on many child abuse cases—including multiple sexual abuse cases at the Piramide pre-school (培諾米達幼兒園) first reported in 2022, the Kaikai Case (剴剴案) in 2023, and a sexual abuse case against a minor employee of McDonald’s restaurant in 2024. Shen has criticized the minor protection mechanisms of Chiang’s government and pledged to make child welfare a policy priority. He and other DPP legislators held a press conference in July accusing the Taipei City government of failing to contact relevant agencies and carrying out procedures only out of formality, revealing the necessity for systemic adjustment. Along with other social welfare policies, Shen proposed to establish a Children and Teenager Safety Governing Center (兒少安全治理中心) under the Taipei Research Institute (台北 研 究院) to integrate data from multiple agencies in analyzing major incidents and reviewing policy responses. He has also stated that he will strive to improve the system and well-being of social workers. In response to Shen and other critics, Chiang affirmed that the Taipei City government has strengthened cross-agency networks regarding childcare management. He also proposed a “7+1 Improvement Plan,” which covers measures such as increasing visitation frequency, strengthening childcare professionals’ training, and providing mental health services. Shen’s Surprising Performance and the “Ocean Current” (“Yang Liu”) Image: A large flag reading “Ocean Current” ( 洋流 , “Yang Liu”) waves above supporters at the opening of Puma Shen’s Taipei campaign headquarters. The term has been adopted as a slogan by Puma Shen supporters. (Image source: qhfan ) Given Shen’s image as a political outsider, many have been surprised by the level of support he has received. The “Ocean Current,” or “Yang Liu” (洋流) , which is derived from Shen’s name, illustrates the island-wide popularity of his campaign. One major attribute to the phenomenon could be the shift of policy focus. This refers not only to particular policy proposals, but also Shen’s entire re-branding in the campaign. During multiple campaigning events and media appearances, he has focused extensively on local issues—such as urban planning, social welfare, and education—while downplaying his usual emphasis on defense and foreign interference. Another tactic that has successfully built up Shen’s active support base is his interactions with voters of different generations. His campaign has attracted the younger generation with non-traditional measures. The interactive features of his campaign website illustrate policy proposals to the younger population, who are comfortable with and reliant on digital interface. His campaign team also extended the normal scope of public policy discussions by collaborating with writers, poets, and artists to create magazines . Shen also endeavors to reach independent voters who are concerned about economic issues and skeptical of the two major parties. He invites voters to in-person “soapbox” (肥皂箱) events to directly express their concerns and needs in daily life. He has also attended multiple interviews , including those held by “Pan-Blue” hosts, to expand target audiences and break out of partisan echo chambers. The impressive civic engagement of Shen’s supporters is also a critical factor in the widespread “Ocean Current” phenomenon. It is worth noting that the “Ocean Current” theme started as a grassroot movement initiated by Shen’s supporters. They turned political enthusiasm into community building through designing and distributing campaign merch, coordinating neighborhood gatherings, and participating in policy discussions. The bottom-up mobilization has effectively complemented Shen’s strategy to re-brand and interact outside of the echo chamber, creating an unprecedented political phenomenon. Can DPP Break the “Blue North and Green South”? Image: Chiang Wan-an of the KMT (top) and Puma Shen of the DPP (bottom) . (Source: jamesonwu1972 and qhfan ) The emergence of the “Ocean Current” movement has surprised the capital city, which has historically been a KMT stronghold. Yet, it remains unknown whether Shen can break the pattern of “Blue North and Green South.” In addition to local governance, the upcoming elections could also alter the national political dynamic in Taiwan. While the DPP holds executive power, it has been facing constant political deadlock in the Legislative Yuan (LY), in which a coalition of the KMT and the Taiwan People’s Party (台灣民眾黨) holds the majority. Tension between the Executive Yuan (EY), the LY, and local government has also reached its height after the LY’s budget cuts earlier this year, as some counties and municipalities receive proportionally less funding than others. The upcoming elections will be an opportunity for the DPP to challenge the KMT’s strong hold on local politics—and a fight for the KMT to defend its base by preventing the spillover effect of Shen’s “Ocean Wave” into other mayoral races. The main point: In Taiwan’s current round of “Nine-in-One” local elections scheduled for November 28, the highest profile race is the Taipei mayoral election. The current campaign pits incumbent mayor Chiang Wan-an of the KMT (a reputed descendant of Chiang Kai-shek) against challenger Puma Shen (Shen Bo-yang) of the DPP. Although Taipei is traditionally a “blue” KMT stronghold, Shen has mounted a stronger-than-expected campaign for the capital city’s top job. As the Taipei mayorship is arguably the most prominent elected position in Taiwan aside from the presidency, the outcome of the election could have implications for future island-wide politics. title: Taiwan as a Partner and Leader in Disaster Prevention and Management
zh_title: 台湾作为灾害预防和管理的合作伙伴和领导者
summary: 下载整期 PDF 2026 年，台湾展示了如何优先考虑国内外的防灾、管理和备灾工作。内政部公布的“2026年救灾及汛期整备”计划鼓励跨部门协作，设立偏远地区应急物资和远程通信项目，进一步发展搜救能力。此外，8 月举行的 2026 年汉光演习显示台湾越来越重视对灾害的两级响应：
content:
下载整期 PDF 2026 年，台湾展示了如何优先考虑国内外的防灾、管理和备灾工作。内政部公布的“2026年救灾及汛期整备”计划鼓励跨部门协作，设立偏远地区应急物资和远程通信项目，进一步发展搜救能力。此外，8月份的2026汉光演习表明台湾对两级灾难响应的日益重视：它展示了军队应对危机的能力，以及地方政府和民间通过建立紧急行动中心来应对危机的能力，同时应对互联网速度的大幅下降。最值得注意的是，政府在 7.7 级集集地震（集集大地震或 921 大地震）周年纪念日举办了一年一度的“国家防灾日”，这场 1999 年的灾难导致 2400 人死亡、1 万人受伤、10 万人无家可归。今年的活动重点测试了紧急广播系统（包括手机、电视和广播）和技术，并动员了近 20 万名民间救灾人员和 5000 名急救志愿者进行当地培训。同日，赖清德总统会见台湾外交伙伴，为“世界灾害管理联盟”（WADM）揭牌。
他表示，WADM是“55年来第一个由台湾牵头成立的政府间组织”。这些里程碑使台湾能够加强与美国和欧盟的关系，并与其外交盟友，特别是太平洋地区的盟友建立伙伴关系。因此，台湾可以加强民主友好国家网络，共享灾害管理信息和策略，并确保在灾害发生时保护平民。赖清德总统（中）与世界灾害管理联盟（WADM）成员国代表及其他政府观察员合影。 （来源：Wikimedia Commons） 台湾在防灾方面的国际合作 美国 特朗普政府避免在灾害管理方面扮演世界领导者的角色。这样做留下了一个由中华人民共和国（PRC）等国家填补的权力真空。 2025 年缅甸地震就是一个例子，中国首先提供了货币援助和实地人员援助 — — 相比之下，美国其他组织则较晚做出临时响应。这在很大程度上归因于美国国际开发署（USAID）的虚拟灭绝，否则该机构将接管西方国家的救援。然而，这种趋势与美国在印太地区的长期领导地位背道而驰。
以美国在2004年节礼日海啸后的援助为例：美国军方利用美国国际开发署、农业部和国防部提供的超过8.41亿美元的政府资金提供了人道主义援助。在拜登政府末期，美国行动者在2024年花莲地震后随叫随到提供援助。在基层，捐款是通过台美民间社会组织的筹款活动引导的。台湾公共机构与美国联邦机构的合作

【原文 English Original】
DOWNLOAD FULL ISSUE PDF In 2026, Taiwan has demonstrated how it prioritized disaster prevention, management, and preparedness at home and abroad. The “ 2026 Disaster Response and Flood-Season Preparedness ( 115年救災及汛期整備 )” plan, announced by the Ministry of the Interior (內政部, MOI), encouraged cross-agency collaboration, set up projects for emergency supplies and remote communication for isolated areas, and further developed search and rescue capabilities. Additionally, the 2026 Han Kuang exercises in August showcased Taiwan’s increased attention toward a two-level response to disasters: it demonstrated the military’s ability to respond to crises— as well as the capacity of local governments and civilians to adapt—by establishing emergency operations centers, while dealing with a massive slowdown in internet speed . Most notably, the government hosted its annual “ Disaster Prevention Day ” (國家防災日) on the anniversary of the 7.7-scale Jiji Earthquake ( 集集大地震 or 921大地震 ), a 1999 tragedy that left 2400 deceased, 10,000 injured, and 100,000 homeless. This year, the event featured testing of emergency broadcast systems (including cell phones, television, and radio) and technology, as well as the mobilization of almost 200,000 civilian disaster responders, plus 5000 volunteer first responders, for local training. On that same day, President Lai Ching-Te ( 賴清德) met with Taiwan’s diplomatic partners, inaugurating the “ World Alliance for Disaster Management ” ( 世界災害管理聯盟, WADM). He stated that the WADM is the “first intergovernmental organization spearheaded and established by Taiwan in 55 years.” These milestones allow Taiwan to strengthen its relations with the US and European Union (EU), and partner with its diplomatic allies, especially those in the Pacific. Thus, Taiwan can strengthen a network of democratic friendly nations, share information and strategies for disaster management, and ensure civilians’ protection in disaster scenarios. President Lai Ching-Te (center) with representatives from member states of the World Alliance for Disaster Management (WADM) and other governmental observers. (Source: Wikimedia Commons ) Taiwan’s International Cooperation in Disaster Prevention The United States The Trump Administration has avoided acting as a world leader in disaster management. In doing so, it has left a vacuum of authority that has been filled by countries such as the People’s Republic of China (PRC). The 2025 Myanmar earthquake is an example, where the PRC was first in providing monetary aid, and on-the-ground personnel assistance –compared to the late, ad-hoc response of remaining US organizations. This was largely attributed to the United States Agency for International Development’s (USAID) virtual extinction , which otherwise would have taken the reins in providing relief from the West. This trend, however, is contrary to the US’ long history of leadership in the Indo-Pacific. Take, for example, the US’ assistance in the wake of the Boxing Day Tsunami in 2004: the US military provided humanitarian aid, utilizing more than USD 841 million in government funding from USAID, the Department of Agriculture, and the Department of Defense. At the tail end of the Biden Administration, US actors were on call to provide assistance following the 2024 Hualien earthquake. At the grassroots level, donations were directed through fundraising efforts by Taiwanese American civil society organizations . Public Taiwanese collaboration with the US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) has been limited to superficial signaling, with the sole instance of in-person activity being the invitation of the National Science and Technology Center for Disaster Reduction (國家災害防救科技中心, NCDR) to the 2018 National Level Exercise International Observer Program. While some of Taiwan’s disaster-focused institutions, such as the Taiwan Community Emergency Response Team (臺灣民間自主緊急應變隊, T-CERT), are based on FEMA initiatives, these counterparts are facing opposite fortunes when it comes to government relevancy in their home countries. The American organization is facing top-down pressure as executive calls continue for states to take up the mantle of local emergency response. Recently, though, the US and Taiwan’s disaster management partnerships have found a new level, operating with the help of various US state entities. The Taipei Economic and Cultural Office (TECO) in Miami met in March with the Florida Division of Emergency Management to discuss “collaboration on disaster management and resilience initiatives.” Even in the first year of the Trump Administration, Taiwan itself highlighted its outward viewpoint as the US was turning inward: TECO in Houston donated 350,000 USD to relief efforts in the aftermath of the debilitating 2025 Texas floods. Civil society on both sides are also facilitating funding or garnering support for local and global disaster management initiatives. American NGOs such Spirit of America are helping fund a “ mesh network of communications ” across the island, and a drone training program to boot. Across the Pacific, The Taiwan-Asia Exchange Foundation (台灣亞洲交流基金會, TAEF) is helping facilitate inter-civil society organization (CSO) dialogue and stronger cross-sector partnerships. The non-governmental aspect should especially be emphasized, noting that the actions of some other countries’ NGOs remain firmly influenced by state desires. It goes without saying that Washington understands Taipei’s importance to the US from an economic and geopolitical point of view. Nevertheless, a natural disaster might create the same consequences as a foreign attack , thereby putting critical industries and supply chain nodes at risk. The European Union Taiwan’s relations with the Europe and the EU in particular rest on the the ideals of common democratic values , and is marked in economic terms by the ties between Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC, 台灣積體電路製造公司 ) and the European Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (ESMC). In terms of disaster prevention and civil defense, the European Parliament has recognized Taiwan’s “whole-of-society resilience” initiative in the face of PRC coercion. Additionally, a group of organizations concerned with resilience initiatives—the European Economic and Trade Office in Taiwan (EETO), Forward Alliance (a Taiwanese think tank for civil defense), and Samaritan International (a European-based NGO network)— met in September this year to workshop civilian solutions to disasters in both areas. Lutz Gullner, head of the EETO, called Taiwan “one of the reference points for anything related to natural disasters”, citing their expertise. Diplomatic Allies in the Pacific Taiwan’s allies in the Pacific are already suffering from some of the worst effects of climate change. In response, Taiwan has organized international action pathways: along with the US, Taiwan hosted a Global Cooperation and Training Framework (GCTF) workshop “Disaster Management in the Pacific” in New Zealand, bringing about public-private partnerships from a host of Pacific-facing countries. It also highlighted Taiwan’s technical and logistical capabilities in combatting earthquakes, hurricanes, and floods, and its practices and resources that can be shared across the Indo-Pacific. In Tuvalu, Taiwan worked with the US under the Biden Administration to fund climate response projects . While these initiatives have faded in Trump’s second term , Taiwan can still assume a leading role in organizing similar plurilateral funding projects for its island partners across the Pacific, using its own history and experience of natural disaster recovery as a diplomatic strategy. Challenges to Taiwan’s Growing Role in Disaster Management The PRC pressures Taiwan, limiting its international partnerships in all sectors. In the field of disaster management, this manifests in Beijing having long blocked Taiwan’s full membership in the World Health Organization (WHO). It has also used its network of state-funded, controlled, and affiliated media to advocate for its global leadership role, showing off Chinese progress in “global disaster governance” during International Day for Disaster Reduction on October 13. Furthermore, the PRC’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI, 一帶一路) features the “ Belt and Road International Cooperation Mechanism for Disaster Risk Reduction and Emergency Management ” ( 一帶一路自然災害防治與緊急管理國際合作機制 ,), which aims to increase investment and good governance measures with regards to combating the risk of disasters in affiliated nations. However, the PRC’s history of humanitarian work has not been consistent, as shown by examples across Asia, and is often tied to its own resource security . China’s disaster help in Southeast Asia has been tinged by conditional questions of South China Sea sovereignty in the case of the Philippines, and for Indonesia , claims of restrained help. China has also failed to fully address domestic disaster relief, such as the cases of flash floods on the Tibet-Nepal border earlier this year. While China did provide emergency supplies and cash assistance to the Nepali government, much more could have been done proactively to mitigate the effects of the disaster, or at least work with authorities to evacuate locals beforehand. Moreover, Beijing concealed the extent of the damage on the Tibetan side. In this regard, inviting the PRC’s assistance in disaster relief is akin to inviting Beijing to pursue initiatives that prioritize the flow of at-risk goods into Chinese hands. Thus, Taiwan can promote its less conditional and more equitable framework for disaster assistance. Policy Recommendations Based on the aforementioned, Taiwan should: 1. Expand the World Alliance for Disaster Management The Ministry of Foreign Affairs (外交部, MOFA) should seek to expand the number of observers and partners of the WADM beyond the likes of the United States, Japan, Poland, and the Philippines. This momentum should be harnessed to gather support from the free world, and counter the pressure of China’s similar organizations, incentivizing non-interventionist support for countries’ disaster preparation. 2. Strengthen Initiatives of Disaster Prevention and Management with the United States Taiwan should invite US federal and local representatives to future iterations of Disaster Prevention Day , to exchange insights and lessons learned in this field. Furthermore, while the 2026 Han Kuang exercises officially featured American observers , these were featured mainly in military components. Taiwanese disaster management personnel should play a role in directly inviting American guests and other willing participants to take part in civilian components, too. Having friendly observers thinking about, and even participating in a whole-of-society Taiwanese response—to include managing severed communication lines, rescuing those in isolated areas, or even an evacuation of the president—by experiencing it firsthand is critical experience that can help the US and others respond most effectively in a time of need. The MOI should seek to work further with FEMA to drum up support, exchange techniques and capabilities, and partner on research initiatives for disaster prevention and management. Organizing collaboration with the National Disaster and Emergency Management University ( NDEMU ) would help both sides strengthen communication and the ability to move populations before disasters strike. Encouraging a reversal of the Trump Administration’s push to minimize national response funding is key for getting their assistance in case of any Taiwan contingency. In this same vein, funding can be delegated to cooperation through civil society organizations, and to joint training of T-CERT with American equivalents and other interested parties. This does not mean, though, that Taiwan should ignore US states’ willingness to cooperate. On a subnational level, Taiwan should locate more places to host private and public events—not just in cities with a TECO Office like San Francisco or Seattle, but also in smaller municipalities across the Pacific, Atlantic, and the Gulf of Mexico. A focus should be placed on liaison activities such as those conducted by the TECO Miami office with the Florida government. Workshops with American locales and further local governments across Asia and the Pacific should highlight Taiwan’s disaster response strengths, and encourage these places to exchange best strategies for preparation and real time response. 3. Seek Further Collaboration with the European Union Given the experience of the EU, Taiwan should seek opportunities for collaboration regarding the use of nuclear power and other energy sources that allow self sufficiency under threatening conditions. It should take advantage of a changing culture around nuclear energy , even if the reasons for this are not expressly from a disaster response point of view. It can also look to co-fund projects within its borders with interested EU partners–expanding the reach of, for example, the National Fire Agency (消防署, NFA), which has sought to expand its assistance into the larger Indo-Pacific region . Additionally, in light of the European Parliament’s language supporting “contingency planning” for Taiwan, MOFA should seek more detailed agreements with the EU (or even willing individual nations such as the Baltic states ). Such agreements could cover a number of functional areas, to include infrastructure reconstruction and food security. 4. Sign MOUs with Pacific Allies Taiwan should sign memoranda of understanding with Pacific research and development-based partners, collaborating with experts who know of specific islands’ vulnerabilities—thereby strengthening Taiwan’s position in the region amid PRC pressure, and further building connections with its diplomatic allies in the region. It can target both academic groups such as the University of Auckland’s Pacific Climate Research Team, as well independent organizations like the Pacific Resilience Partnership . In the same vein, it should look to monitor and get involved in up-to-now bilateral frameworks for tsunami relief, such as in the case of Hawaii and Samoa’s National Disaster Preparedness Baseline Assessment (NDPBA). Conclusion Natural and geopolitical factors compel Taiwan to be ready for disasters. However, Taiwanese people are not isolated from the goodwill of the rest of the world. Given its geography and aforementioned history, Taiwan has the capabilities to become a reliable partner in disaster management around the world. Taiwan should leverage its capabilities and share its expertise, thereby strengthening both its own resilience and its relationships across the democratic world. The main point: Taiwan should further collaborate with the US and the EU with regards to disaster prevention and management, especially utilizing its mastery of subnational and civil society-based diplomacy, while taking a leadership role in disaster preparation and as a research collaborator amongst its diplomatic partners in the Pacific. This outreach will help skirt the challenges it faces in terms of pressure on the global stage.
